reference.source: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
clinicalPearls: Brittle nail syndrome describes nails that split, flake, crumble or break easily, and is common, affecting a large proportion of adults and women more than men.
Two morphological patterns are recognised: onychoschizia, a lamellar splitting of the free edge into horizontal layers, and onychorrhexis, longitudinal ridging and splitting.
The dominant mechanism is repeated cycles of hydration and dehydration, worsened by frequent hand washing, wet work and exposure to detergents, solvents and nail cosmetics.
It may be idiopathic and age-related or secondary to dermatoses such as lichen planus and psoriasis, or to systemic factors including iron deficiency and thyroid disease.
A careful history should explore occupational and domestic wet work, cosmetic and solvent exposure, and any relevant systemic symptoms.

Management emphasises protecting the nails, minimising water and irritant exposure, regular emollient and the consistent use of emollients or nail hydrating agents; supplementation is reserved for demonstrated deficiency.
Biotin supplementation has traditional support for nail fragility, but it can interfere with several laboratory immunoassays and should be noted before testing.
The condition is chiefly one of quality of life and cosmesis rather than a threat to health, though it can be a clue to underlying disease.
reference.pathophysiology: The nail plate depends for its strength on the orderly adhesion of corneocytes and on an appropriate water and lipid content. In brittle nail syndrome this integrity is disturbed, most often by repeated wetting and drying that fatigues the intercellular bonds between the layered keratinocytes of the plate, so that the distal nail delaminates (onychoschizia) or splits along its long axis (onychorrhexis). Reduced cohesion may also follow matrix disease that produces a structurally poor plate, as in lichen planus, or from generalised nail thinning with age. Nutritional deficiency, particularly of iron, and endocrine disturbance such as thyroid dysfunction can further impair keratinisation. The common final pathway is a plate with diminished flexibility and cohesion that fractures under normal mechanical stress.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and ferritin for iron deficiency
Nail clipping for mycology to exclude onychomycosis
Dermoscopy of the nail plate and folds
Assessment for signs of lichen planus or psoriasis elsewhere
redFlags: Brittleness confined to a single nail or with a subungual mass, raising concern for a tumour
Associated nail dystrophy with scarring suggesting lichen planus
Systemic features such as fatigue and pallor pointing to iron deficiency or thyroid disease
Rapidly progressive dystrophy of all nails
reference.prognosis: Brittle nail syndrome is benign but often chronic and relapsing, improving with consistent protective measures and correction of any underlying cause. Because nails grow slowly, visible improvement typically takes several months.
pitfalls: Prescribing biotin without noting its interference with laboratory immunoassays such as thyroid and troponin testing
Overlooking onychomycosis or nail dermatoses as the true cause of fragility
Failing to check for iron deficiency or thyroid disease in appropriate patients
Expecting rapid improvement rather than the several months dictated by nail growth

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
management: Protect the nails by minimising wet work and exposure to detergents, solvents, and nail cosmetics, wearing gloves for household and occupational tasks
Apply emollients and nail hydrating agents regularly, ideally after soaking, to restore water and lipid content
Keep nails short and file rather than cut the free edge to reduce delamination and splitting
Correct any demonstrated underlying cause, giving iron for iron deficiency and treating thyroid dysfunction
Trial oral biotin supplementation, which may improve nail plate strength in some patients
Treat associated nail dermatoses such as lichen planus or psoriasis where identified
Counsel that improvement is gradual over months because nails grow slowly
